title: Today's Gates Notes on AI And Why I Started Education Disrupted
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Stefan Bauschard uses Bill Gates's newly published essay on the "turbulent AI era" as the occasion to explain the founding premise of his own newsletter, Education Disrupted. He argues that AI's classroom impact on assignments and assessment, the disruption that got the earliest attention from educators, is actually the smaller of two disruptions AI will cause. The larger one is societal: because schools exist to prepare students for work and citizenship in the world as it actually is, and AI is set to reshape entire industries like law, medicine, and manufacturing within a decade rather than generations, the true reckoning for education is that the target itself is moving faster than schools can adapt. Bauschard positions this as the reason his newsletter treats AI as an education story even when it looks like industry or society news.
points: Distinguishes two distinct AI disruptions to education: the immediate, well-covered one (assignments and assessment) and the larger, under-discussed one (society and the economy schools prepare students for).
Quotes Gates's framing that AI will not just affect one sector but will hit law, customer service, medicine, software, and manufacturing rapidly, over a decade rather than a few generations.
Argues schools cannot treat AI purely as an ed-tech tooling problem, because 'change the world and you've changed the assignment, whether or not anyone in the building has noticed.'
Frames the core institutional risk as a pacing mismatch: the world AI is reshaping moves in a decade, but schools historically have not moved that fast.
quotes: AI will either be the greatest equalizer ever invented, or the worst source of injustice. We have no experience with a technology that can be adopted quickly or that can think and move like a human.

Because it can see, listen, speak, and reason and will eventually do physical work just as smoothly as any human, it will not just affect one sector. AI will take on work in law, customer service, medicine, software, and manufacturing.

The first was obvious: this was going to disrupt education directly. Assignments, assessment, what we ask students to produce, what any of it measures. That's the version that got all the early attention, and it's the smaller of the two.

Schools don't exist in isolation. They exist to prepare people for a world, for work, for citizenship, for the specific set of things adults need to be able to do. Change the world and you've changed the assignment, whether or not anyone in the building has noticed.
If the shape of that work moves in a decade, the preparation has to move too, and schools have never moved in a decade.
